documents.abstract: _ This case study from Tomax outlines the use of artificial intelligence to analyze high-fidelity data of the full drilling process. The problem of downhole vibrations remains a significant barrier for the drilling industry. An emerging technology based on direct interception of disturbing resonances is now being used to address the issue. Such solutions rely on a new level of understanding with respect to the true bottomhole assembly (BHA) dynamics. Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) techniques are now helping deliver the full picture. While the specific product development in this field belongs in the commercial space, the necessity for more and better data on drilling dynamics is commonplace. This case study describes a successful solution for data harvesting on a level that is both new and found to meet requirement for the application of AI/ML solutions. The study concludes with examples from analysis that reveal the potential from a true image of everything going on in a drillstring. Reinventing Drilling Dynamics Traditional analysis of drilling dynamics frequently references data from downhole accelerometers. However, these systems typically capture a mix of effects rather than the underlying coupling of forces that cause resonances and, consequently, poor performance and downtime from failures. The fundamentals of these resonances reside in the transfer of torsional and axial forces from surface to the bit. On most rigs, the surface input and reactive loads are recorded at sparse intervals (typically every 10 seconds or longer). Capturing this critical information at a high-fidelity level in this environment presents two critical challenges: - Signal Integrity: Eliminating data corruption and packet loss from intermittent transfer when sampling frequencies exceeding 1,000 Hz using RF from a rotating shaft in a rough environment. - Data Pipeline: While modern sensor assemblies can export structural acoustics and stress waves at extreme sample rates, the bottleneck is the data pipeline and the requirement for a continuous stream of megabytes of time-stamped data every second into a usable database.

UV–Visible (UV–Vis) spectrophotometry is a rapid, economical and widely available technique for pharmaceutical analysis, but its selectivity is limited when the drugs in a formulation have overlapping absorption spectra. The integration of chemometrics and artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) algorithms such as partial least squares (PLS), principal component regression (PCR), support vector regression (SVR), artificial neural networks (ANN) and random forests, with intelligent wavelength selection and metaheuristic optimization (genetic and Firefly algorithms), allows the simultaneous quantification of several active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) from the whole spectrum rather than a single wavelength. This review summarizes the principles of UV–Vis spectroscopy, the current status of AI-assisted UV–Vis analysis, and the challenges related to model interpretability, data integrity, validation and instrument variability. Applications, drawbacks and futureprospects are discussed, including process analytical technology (PAT), portable instruments, green analytical chemistry and regulatory acceptance of AI-enabled spectroscopic methods as complementary tools to chromatographic assays in pharmaceutical quality control.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: Software development often requires programmers to write repetitive code, understand unfamiliar requirements, and spend considerabletime identifying and correcting errors. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have enabled systems to generate source code fromnatural-language instructions. However, generated code may contain syntax errors, incorrect logic, insecure patterns, or incompletehandling of edge cases. This paper proposes an AI-Based Code Generation and Self-Testing System that accepts a programming task innatural language, generates a candidate solution, prepares or selects test cases, executes the code in a controlled environment, and analysesthe results. The proposed workflow combines prompt interpretation, code generation, static validation, test-case generation, sandboxedexecution, and feedback-based refinement. The system is intended to support developers and learners by reducing repetitive effort andproviding an initial validation cycle. It does not replace code review or guarantee correctness; execution safety, test coverage, modellimitations, and human verification remain important. This paper presents a proposed methodology and evaluation plan. Quantitativeperformance claims should be added only after implementation and testing.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered customer service systems have expanded across Saudi Arabia’s retail sector during 2025–2026, with major retailers increasingly exploring chatbots, recommendation engines, and automated service technologies. Official Saudi digital-economy statistics document the wider shift towards digital commerce, although online-shopping participation should not be interpreted as a direct measure of AI adoption or retailer-specific investment. This study examines the relationship among AI service quality, emotional brand attachment, and brand loyalty using survey results reported for 512 retail customers in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam, collected between May and September 2026. Using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and bootstrap resampling, the analysis reports a positive direct association between AI service quality and loyalty (β = 0.421, p < 0.001), together with a positive indirect association through emotional brand attachment (reported indirect effect = 0.238, 95% CI [0.187, 0.289]). The study considers a possible “mechanical efficiency paradox”: functional improvements in AI service may be more strongly associated with loyalty than with emotional attachment. Importantly, this survey does not include a direct comparison with human-delivered service, and the reported positive attachment coefficient (β = 0.187) cannot establish that AI decreases attachment. The reported gender subgroup estimates differ: the AI quality–attachment association is positive for male respondents (β = 0.289, p = 0.001) and statistically nonsignificant for female respondents (β = −0.023, p = 0.811). Age-specific estimates also vary, with more positive reported coefficients in younger groups, although the statistical significance of the age differences requires further supporting output. The manuscript reports that the model accounts for 51.2% of the variance in loyalty (R2 = 0.512) and has positive predictive relevance (Q2 = 0.289). Because some path estimates, correlations, and variance-explained values are not mutually consistent, these results require rechecking against the original SmartPLS output before publication. Managerial implications include offering hybrid AI–human service, allowing customers to choose their preferred channel, and maintaining personal attention for complex or emotionally sensitive interactions. The findings provide a framework for assessing how technological service quality and relationship-building might jointly contribute to brand loyalty.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Pharmaceutical marketing is being reshaped by the growing use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) in communication, customer engagement, and commercial decision-making. Promotion that once relied almost entirely on medical representatives, face-to-face physician visits, product detailing, and printed material is now supplemented, and in some cases reshaped, by digital platforms, social media, e-detailing, webinars, data analytics, and omnichannel communication. This review looks at how AI is being applied to pharmaceutical digital marketing, with particular attention to machine learning, predictive analytics, segmentation of customers and healthcare professionals, personalized communication, customer relationship management, generative AI, and omnichannel engagement. Evidence from the published literature suggests that digital channels widen the reach and flexibility of pharmaceutical communication, while AI adds the ability to analyse large datasets, anticipate behaviour, segment audiences, and personalize content at scale. At the same time, this shift brings its own set of problems: data privacy, inconsistent data quality, algorithmic bias, the risk of misinformation, limited transparency, regulatory compliance, and the continued need for human oversight all surface repeatedly in the literature. Empirical studies also indicate that digital engagement can shape how healthcare professionals are communicated with, influence prescribing-related behaviour, and affect consumer attitudes, though the size of this effect depends heavily on the channel, audience, and therapeutic area involved. Taken together, the evidence points toward a future in which human expertise, digital communication, and AI-supported decision-making work alongside one another rather than one replacing the other. For this model to be sustainable, pharmaceutical marketing will need to be built on responsible implementation, ethical communication, evidence-based content, and clear governance.

Practical writing is an important component of senior high school English teaching. he English Curriculum Standards for Senior High School (2017 edition, 2020 revision) requires students to select appropriate language forms according to the identity of the communicative partner, he occasion and the degree of formality, o as to achieve effective cross-cultural communication. owever, urrent practical writing teaching in Grade 10 still suffers from mechanical format training, eak reader awareness, nappropriate register control, nd single and delayed feedback. Although generative artificial intelligence offers new possibilities for writing instruction, existing studies have focused mainly on automated essay scoring, academic writing at the tertiary level, or continuation writing tasks, and few have systematically constructed an AI-empowered mechanism and teaching pathway for senior high school practical writing from the perspective of the integration of teaching, learning and assessment. Adopting a conceptual construction and lesson design orientation, and grounded in the cognitive process theory of writing,t he technology-enhanced language learning framework, self-efficacy theory and formative assessment theory, this study proposes a “5A+E” empowerment mechanism model, comprising Analysis, Activation, Assistance, Assessment, Adaptation, and Ethics. On this basis, a five-stage teaching pathway—context trigger, element deconstruction, AI co-writing, multi-dimensional evaluation, and reflective transfer—is designed, and a lesson on the invitation letter for the “Chinese Culture Festival” is presented. The study argues that AI can serve as a reader analyst, format validator, point generator, register regulator and evaluation embedder, moving practical writing instruction from template drilling toward authentic communication. As a theoretical construction and lesson design study, this paper has not yet been empirically tested; future action research or quasi-experimental studies are needed to validate and refine the model and pathway.

Grievance redressal is where citizens test whether government listens. Indian governments receive millions of complaints each year through portals, call centres, social media, letters and in-person visits. The volume, the variety of languages and the number of departments involved make it hard to route complaints correctly, resolve them on time and learn from patterns. Artificial intelligence (AI), and in particular natural language processing for Indian languages, can help with each of these steps — but only if it is introduced with clear safeguards and with officers, not algorithms, remaining accountable for decisions. This paper proposes a five-layer framework for AI-enabled grievance redressal in Indian states: (1) multilingual, multichannel intake; (2) classification, routing and prioritisation; (3) officer assistance for resolution; (4) closure verification and citizen feedback; and (5) analytics for root-cause and policy learning. For each layer it sets out what AI can do, the human checks required and suitable performance measures. It also discusses governance, data protection and change-management requirements, and suggests a phased path from pilot to state-wide adoption. The paper is a design framework drawn from e-governance practice and the published literature; it does not report results from a deployed system.

The continued growth of mobile data traffic is placing increasing demands on radio access networks (RANs).Although 4G and 5G networks already use sophisticated automation to manage radio resources, conventionaloptimisation methods can struggle to respond efficiently to rapidly changing traffic patterns, complex interferenceconditions and variations in user behaviour. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer an opportunityto make network management more predictive by identifying patterns in network data, forecasting demand andsupporting more adaptive resource allocation. This article examines the development of AI-native RAN, focusing onthe UK 5G environment. It reviews radio resource management, predictive optimisation and emerging AI-RANarchitectures, including the O-RAN Intelligent Controller framework. It considers the O2–Nokia live deploymentannounced at London Paddington in October 2026 and BT's planned AI-RAN trial with Nokia and NVIDIA inBirmingham during 2027. It also examines data quality, model reliability, security, interoperability, computingoverhead and human oversight. The article argues that AI-native RAN should be treated as an evolution ofestablished radio engineering, with benefits demonstrated through measurable improvements in network efficiency,reliability and customer experience.

This paper provides a comprehensive critical analysis of algorithmic bias in human resource management, examining how artificial intelligence (AI) systems used in hiring, promotions, and performance management can perpetuate and amplify societal biases. Moving beyond conventional discussions of bias, this research introduces a series of novel theoretical frameworks to uncover the deeper, systemic mechanisms through which algorithmic HR systems produce inequitable outcomes. These include the Sociotechnical Bias Amplification Model (SBAM), which explains how temporal bias, intersectional bias, and feedback loops interact to compound discrimination; the Algorithmic Opacity Paradox, which argues that the perceived objectivity of AI obscures its discriminatory potential; and the Fairness Impossibility Theorem in the HR context, which demonstrates the mathematical and normative trade-offs inherent in any algorithmic fairness definition. The paper further develops a critical perspective by introducing concepts such as data colonialism, the performance management panopticon, and the algorithmic accountability gap. Through a synthesis of technical literature, organizational theory, and critical algorithm studies, this research argues that the challenge of algorithmic bias is not merely a technical problem of “debiasing” but a fundamental crisis of legitimacy for automated decision-making in the workplace. The analysis is supported by clearly labelled conceptual diagrams and selected empirical findings drawn from published research. It concludes with a set of actionable recommendations for HR leaders, policymakers, and researchers, advocating for a shift from a technical-fix mindset to a more holistic, human-centered approach to governance that prioritizes justice, accountability, and equity.

documents.abstract: This review assesses ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention and slope stabilization by synthesizing evidence identified through scientific databases. The review encompasses the idea of applying vegetation-based techniques, including live stakes, brush layering, revegetation, grasses, herbaceous plants, bamboo plantations, and lithophytic life forms, together with conventional and structural measures such as natural geotextiles, live wooden crib walls, wattle fences, live silt fences, and live gully breaks. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of species with strong root systems, which can influence the effectiveness of bioengineering interventions. Species such as Vetiver, Bermuda Grass, Ryegrass, Alder, selected Ficus species, and bamboo show deep-rooted control over soil reinforcement, erosion, and slope stabilization, while lithophytic life forms and pioneer colonizers may support the restoration of exposed rocky and landslide-affected surfaces. The review also examines the contribution of artificial intelligence, remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, LiDAR, interferometric synthetic aperture radar, and machine learning models in landslide susceptibility assessment, monitoring, and advance warning. Overall, the findings revealed that integrated ecological engineering and data-driven monitoring may complement conventional stabilization measures, reduce landslide risk, restore degraded slopes, and inform sustainable land-management planning.

This research is motivated by the high turnover of contract employees in the Operational Division of PT. XYZ which has an impact on increasing recruitment needs, disrupting company operations, and decreasing productivity. The study aims to analyze employee retention factors including organizational components, career opportunities, rewards, job design, and employee relations. The method used is a qualitative approach supported by descriptive analysis using the Weight Mean Score (WMS). Data were collected through observation, questionnaires to 61 contract employees, semi-structured interviews with five informants, and documentation. Data analysis was carried out through data reduction, data presentation, drawing conclusions, and WMS analysis. The results of the study indicate that all factors are in the good category, namely organizational components (3.66), career opportunities (3.58), rewards (3.68), job design (3.62), and employee relations (3.52). However, the company still needs to improve work facilities, transparency of promotions and career paths, fairness of rewards, job variety, and communication between superiors and employees. The study concludes that these five factors contribute to supporting contract employee retention at PT. XYZ.

This study investigates the implementation of Management Information Systems (MIS) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic education governance at MIN 9 Magetan. Driven by digital transformation demands, the research aims to analyze the integration of these technologies, identify supporting and inhibiting factors, and evaluate their impact on educational service quality. Employing a qualitative case study design, data were collected through observations, in-depth interviews, and documentation, and analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings reveal that the deployment of specific MIS platforms, such as EMIS 4.0 and ERKAM, significantly enhances administrative efficiency, financial transparency, and data-driven decision-making by the madrasah leadership. Concurrently, the grassroots adoption of AI tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini, and Canva AI, empowers teachers to accelerate lesson planning, design Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) assessments, and foster pedagogical innovation through interactive learning media. While visionary leadership commitment and adequate digital infrastructure strongly support this transformation, several challenges persist. These include a digital literacy gap among senior educators experiencing cultural resistance, as well as operational disruptions caused by central server instability during critical data synchronization periods. Ultimately, the synergistic integration of MIS and AI positively impacts service quality, transparency, and accountability. Therefore, prioritizing targeted digital literacy programs and allocating dedicated budgets for comprehensive AI training are recommended to ensure sustainable implementation. This study contributes to the development of a modern Islamic education governance model that harmonizes digital technology, human resource competence, and good governance principles grounded in Islamic values.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning (ML) are two terms that transformed pharmaceutical sciences, including drug discovery, drug development, precision medicine and nanomedicine. Traditional drug discovery is a long, expensive and failure-prone process that may take over 10 years and million of dollars before it produces a therapeutically active compound ready for clinical trials and commercialization. AI-driven computational approaches can tackle numerous challenges of drug discovery and development, including target or lead identification and optimization, virtual screening, predicting drug target interactions, toxicity and personalized treatment options. The concept of artificial intelligence was first introduced in the 1940s when Alan Turing laid the foundations for machine intelligence theory claiming that there is no fundamental difference between human and machine computation (Turing, 1950). The formal idea of artificial intelligence was further proposed by Mc Carthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon who proposed the Dartmouth Hypothesis about the possibility for machines to stimulate human intelligence (Mc Carthy et al 1955). In the following decades the concepts machine learning and deep learning were introduced Schmidhuber in 2015. There are three review papers that discuss the role of AI&ML in pharmaceutical sciences and health care. The first study focus on the role of artificial intelligence in drug discovery and discovery and precision nanomedicine (Zhu et al, 2022). Zhu et al. highlight importance of algorithms and nano-enabled therapeutics for precision nanomedicine. The main ideas of the study include finding and selecting the target developing the optimal drug using nano-enabled therapeutics and individualizing treatment based on patients characteristics. The second review paper discuss the role of AI in spatial structure of protein predicting and drug synergism prediction targeting molecular mechanism and protein drug interactions (Lie et al, 2022). The study by Lei et al. high-light the importance of AI in analyzing and prediction the spatial structure of protein to reveal molecular mechanisms and biological functions. The third review paper was discusses the concept of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning elucidates ethical and social implications and high light the public awarness about AI (Garcia & Salichos, 2022). The study by Garcia & Salichosis a detailed analysis about the opportunities and limitations of AI.I would like to address the main ideas of all three reviewed papers and discuss hoe AL&ML can be applied to various stages of drug discovery and development. I will also comment on such terms as machine learning, deep learning, protein spatial structure prediction, virtual screening precision, precision medicine, nanomedicine, drug synergism prediction, explainable AI.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of healthcare through tools that help organise medical information, support clinical decisions, answer common questions, and improve communication. These changes affect more than treatment and efficiency: they can also influence how patients feel, how much they trust healthcare professionals, and whether they feel heard and respected. This paper reviews AI in patient–healthcare relationships from a psychosocial perspective. It considers trust, empathy, privacy, patient autonomy, health literacy, anxiety, accessibility, and the role of clinicians in explaining AI-supported decisions. AI can make some services faster and easier to access, but it may also create distance when communication feels automated or when recommendations are difficult to understand. The paper argues that AI should strengthen—not replace—the human relationship at the centre of care. Responsible use requires transparency, protection of personal information, inclusive design, careful evaluation, and meaningful human oversight..

documents.abstract: This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption on audit quality in emerging economies, with an emphasis on fraud detection, risk assessment, implementation challenges, and the roles of auditor competence and technological readiness. A quantitative research design was employed, using secondary panel data from 25 firms observed over a decade, yielding 250 firm-year observations. Data were drawn from annual reports, audit reports, governance disclosures, and publicly available financial statements. Analytical techniques included descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, fixed- and random-effects regression models, and Hausman specification tests to ensure methodological robustness. Findings reveal that AI adoption significantly enhances audit quality by improving fraud detection and risk assessment, enabling auditors to identify irregularities and unusual transactions more effectively. Nonetheless, weak technological infrastructure, high implementation costs, cybersecurity risks, and limited expertise constrain optimal adoption. Auditor competence and technological readiness emerged as decisive factors influencing AI’s effectiveness in improving audit outcomes. This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence on AI’s transformative role in auditing within emerging economies, highlighting both opportunities and constraints. The findings underscore the need for investments in digital infrastructure, auditor training, and cybersecurity frameworks to maximize AI’s potential in audit practice.

AI tools are increasingly being utilized in counselling services to provide student support, but their impact on undergraduate students needs to be thoroughly examined. This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Counselling Service among Undergraduate Students in Cross River State. To achieve this, three (3) objectives, three (3) research questions and three (3) hypotheses were formulated. Correlational research design was adopted. The sample was 760 students from the sampled faculties out of 44,281 in UNICAL, 31,410 in CRSUE, and 23,971 in UNICROSS. Three experts validated the instrument, it was titled "Usage, Awareness, Attitude towards AI and Effective Counselling Service Questionnaire" and was administered to the respondents to elicit their responses.

This study examines the relationship between the development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and the rights of older persons. It analyses the opportunities that smart applications offer in health care, independent living, social connection and economic security, set against the risks arising from digital exclusion, algorithmic age discrimination, privacy violations and fraud. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach based on international reports, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and relevant national surveys, and discusses the UAE legislative context. The review shows that the age gap in use remains wide, that the evidence of benefits is promising but limited, and that fraud risks are documented by rising figures. The study proposes a preliminary framework for safe digital empowerment that links graduated learning, inclusive design, data protection, human review and evaluation. It concludes that the rights-based value of AI is not measured by the mere availability of a service, but by its capacity to expand the real choices of older persons while respecting their will and dignity. The study does not present field results, nor does it claim to have tested the proposed model. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates religious communication, knowledge, and participation in the digital public sphere, yet research remains fragmented across digital religion, human rights, and AI governance. This study examines how AI-mediated religious communication shapes authority, visibility, and participation; identifies associated ethical and rights-based concerns; and analyzes the institutional conditions relevant to its governance. Using a qualitative, non-experimental, exploratory-analytical design, the study draws on academic publications, policy documents, regulatory instruments, institutional guidelines, human-rights reports, and documented analyses of digital religious practices. Materials were purposively selected for substantive relevance and examined through structured reading and extraction, open and focused coding, thematic synthesis, source triangulation, and iterative cross-source comparison. The analysis identified three interconnected domains: access, visibility, and religious authority; religious freedom, inclusion, and algorithmic risks; and accountability, contestability, and institutional responsibility. AI-mediated technologies can broaden access to religious resources while simultaneously shaping the visibility and perceived authority of religious actors and interpretations. Expanded access can coexist with unequal representation, privacy risks, profiling, and constraints on meaningful participation, while distributed responsibility can create accountability gaps when consequential outcomes are difficult to explain or challenge. These relationships are context-dependent rather than predetermined effects of AI. By integrating sociotechnical and algorithmic-governance perspectives, the study provides an analytical framework for understanding ethical governance as the intersection of technological mediation, religious pluralism, fundamental rights, participation, and identifiable institutional responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This research reveals the contemporary British fiction crisis of human identity through a comparative reading of Kazoo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun and Ian McEwan’s Machines Like Me. Both novels view artificial intelligence as more than just a technology, instead, they treat it as a tool for subverting the human-machine divide. According to Adam, humans do not possess true moral agency, while Klara brings into question the nature of love, care, memory, and social recognition as essential qualities of personhood. By drawing upon the frameworks of critical posthumanism and AI ethics, we can find out that the novels are more concerned with whether human beings are capable of retaining a stable and exceptional identity when affect, consciousness, simulation, and ethical agency become entangled rather than on whether machines can be human. As comparison shows that artifice operates as a mirror through which contemporary fiction exhibits the ethical, emotional and ontological fragility of the human self.

Three-dimensional (3D) printing is a computer-aided, layer-by-layer manufacturing technology with strong potential for personalized medicines. Combined with artificial intelligence (AI), it enables predictive, data-driven development, improving formulation design, process robustness, and quality control. However, evidence remains fragmented across technologies, dosage forms, and computational approaches. This scoping review aimed to map and describe the application of AI to formulation design, manufacturing-process optimization, and quality assessment of pharmaceutical dosage forms and drug-delivery systems produced by 3D printing, including device-assisted delivery systems such as microneedles. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science until November 18, 2025. Original studies applying AI to the design, manufacturing, or quality assessment of 3D-printed drug products or drug–device combinations were included. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and analysis. Findings were synthesized through descriptive tables and narrative analysis. Twenty studies published between 2020 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Technologies included Fused Deposition Modeling, Selective Laser Sintering, Semi-Solid Extrusion, Vat Photopolymerization, and Inkjet Printing. Oral dosage forms and associated formulation or printing workflows predominated; two studies specifically investigated microneedle-based delivery systems. Reported approaches included random forests, support vector machines, artificial neural networks, deep learning, chemometric regression, generative models, Bayesian optimization, and evolutionary algorithms. Applications addressed formulation and printability prediction, processing-condition selection, drug-release modeling, and image-based quality assessment. Individual studies reported potential benefits related to process robustness, experimental effort, and development time; however, differences in study designs, datasets, and outcome definitions limit comparisons and generalization. The review maps applications of AI in formulation design, process optimization, and quality assessment in pharmaceutical 3D printing, without establishing their comparative effectiveness. Future research should prioritize methodological harmonization, standardized validation, and interdisciplinary collaboration to facilitate translation and regulatory acceptance.
topics: Innovations in Concrete and Construction Materials

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and data science are increasingly proposed as ways to extend scarce expertise, interpret complex data, and improve the timing and targeting of services in low- and middle-income countries and other resource-constrained communities. This paper synthesizes recent peer-reviewed studies and institutional guidance across education, healthcare, humanitarian assistance, disaster response, agriculture, and public information management. Evidence shows that carefully bounded systems can perform useful tasks: offline crop-disease screening can assist extension workers; AI-supported diabetic-retinopathy screening can expand diagnostic capacity; machine-learning forecasts can support flood warnings; and data-driven poverty maps or mobile-phone signals can inform social-assistance targeting. Yet predictive accuracy is not equivalent to public benefit. Benefits depend on representative data, local validation, affordable and resilient infrastructure, accessible interfaces, trusted institutions, and human capacity to act on outputs. Comparative evidence is strongest for specific, measurable tasks and substantially weaker for long-term population outcomes and scalable implementation. Major risks include exclusion of people poorly represented in data, proxy-label bias, privacy and surveillance harms, automation overreach, weak redress, and dependence on external platforms. The paper argues for locally led, task-specific, human-accountable AI, evaluated against non-AI alternatives and real service outcomes. It concludes with a research agenda centered on data stewardship, context-sensitive evaluation, accessible deployment, and equitable governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Stretching the integration of renewable energy, energy storage, electric vehicles (EVs) and smart-grid technologies at an unprecedented rate will produce increasingly complex and dynamic power systems that defy conventional optimization and control methods. This paper offers a systematic engineering review of the state of the art and future potential for the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in sustainable and resilient electric power systems, which includes machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning (RL), hybrid AI, explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning (FL), and digital twins (DTs). The review covers their use in renewable energy and load forecasting, energy management, predictive maintenance, demand response, adaptive control, energy storage, smart grid and EV/Vehicle-to-Grid coordination. A single framework based on the grid is presented that integrates predictive intelligence, optimization, adaptive control, cyber-physical systems, explainability, cyber-security, and sustainability in a closed-loop system. The analysis underscores the transformative possibilities of AI in enhancing the use of renewable energy, its efficiency, resilience of the grid and smart decision making. But, deployment needs to address the uncertainties, data quality, computational costs, latency, Cybersecurity, interoperability, scalability, model drift, and regulatory needs. The review also highlights Green AI to tackle the energy and carbon footprint of increasingly large AI models. Lastly, physics-informed and uncertainty-aware AI, safe RL, DT-assisted validation, edge intelligence, FL and real-world benchmarking are identified as key directions for next-generation power systems to remain trustworthy and sustainable.

Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

documents.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly statistical machine learning (ML), can complement established econometric approaches to inflation forecasting and macroeconomic analysis. Inflation is a difficult prediction target because it is measured with delay, revised in some datasets, driven by multiple interacting forces, and subject to structural change. Linear time-series and structural models remain valuable because they encode persistence, economic mechanisms, and interpretable scenarios. ML methods can add value where information sets are wide, relationships are nonlinear, interactions matter, or data arrive in mixed formats. The central question is therefore not whether Al replaces econometrics, but when and under what validation conditions it improves a policy-relevant forecast. A literature-based synthesis reviews foundational inflation forecasting research, contemporary ML studies, central-bank applications, and institutional data sources. The evidence is conditional. Data-rich ML models improved on selected benchmarks in a prominent U.S. application, yet later replications found that relative performance changes across countries, benchmarks, methods, and episodes. An ECB quantile-regression-forest application found small advantages for core inflation but mixed results for headline inflation. Text embeddings of central-bank communication have also shown forecast information in one euro-area application, although this remains specialized evidence. Broader IMF and OECD studies on output growth and GDP nowcasting are discussed as adjacent, not direct, inflation evidence.

documents.abstract: This study examined the influence of Fairness, Transparency, and Accountability [FTA] on student acceptance of Artificial Intelligence [AI] in higher education institutions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Grounded on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, data were collected from 240 undergraduate students from six universities using a structured 5-point likert scale questionnaire. Descriptive analysis and Pearson correlation were conducted using SPSS v26. Results indicated that students reported moderately high acceptance of AI for learning but low perceptions of fairness, transparency, and accountability. Transparency emerged as the most critical concern, with 45-50% of students reporting limited understanding of AI decision-making processes. Correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between all three FTA dimensions and student acceptance. The findings suggest that while perceived usefulness drives initial adoption, ethical concerns may hinder sustainable use. The study recommends that Pakistani HEIs implement bias-free AI systems, provide explainable AI interfaces, and establish clear accountability structures to build student trust. This study contributes to AI ethics literature in the Pakistani context and provides implications for policymakers and university administrators.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping customer engagement, yet its influence on consumer behavior within hospitality and tourism services remains underexplored.This study examines the associations among AI-enabled engagement, digital marketing, and consumer behavior in hospitality and tourism contexts.Survey data were collected from 221 respondents and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) in an exploratory capacity.The measurement analysis revealed that AI, digital marketing, and consumer behavior are very strongly interrelated: inter-construct correlations were high (AI-DM r = 0.871; DM-CB r = 0.882) and exceeded the square roots of the average variance extracted, so the three constructs did not achieve discriminant validity under the Fornell-Larcker criterion.Rather than interpreting this as a mediation mechanism, the study treats it as a substantive finding: in this hospitality and tourism setting, consumers appear to experience AI, the digital marketing it enables, and their own engagement responses as a single, tightly coupled digitalengagement domain rather than as separable constructs.Model fit was marginal (RMSEA = 0.113; CFI = 0.870), so all relationships are reported as indicative and associational rather than causal.The study contributes contextually by situating AI within hospitality and tourism service ecosystems and by documenting the strong convergence of these digital-engagement constructs, offering guidance for hospitality organizations and advancing discourse on sustainable, human-centered tourism strategies aligned with logistics, informatics, and service science.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful tool in various aspects of our daily lives. One of the most particular areas revolutionized by AI is medicine. Reproductive medicine is no exception to this integration. A narrative review was conducted to evaluate the current applications of AI-powered tools in the management of infertility. Searches were performed on October 25th, 2025, in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Embase, Cochrane Library, and IEEE Xplore using predefined keywords and Boolean operators. After duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, original English-language studies relevant to AI-assisted infertility management were included for analysis. Our search identified 18 studies published between 2013 and 2025. Embryo selection and implantation prediction in in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) were the most common applications (8 studies), with AI models demonstrating superior performance compared to embryologists in several studies. The STORK deep neural network also demonstrated high accuracy in blastocyst quality assessment, while machine learning models showed promise in predicting ovarian reserve and fertilization outcomes. Other applications included ovarian stimulation optimization (3 studies), male infertility assessment (2 studies), and broader reproductive outcomes including live birth and miscarriage prediction (5 studies). AI shows promising potential to support infertility management by improving embryo selection, ovarian stimulation, assessment of male infertility, and broader reproductive outcomes. To ensure safe clinical adoption, future work must prioritize multi-center prospective trials, transparency, and standardized frameworks.

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyse the existing literature and identify major research trends in artificial intelligence in logistics service quality research.Data were retrieved from the Scopus database, comprising 281 journal articles and review papers published between 2002 and 2026, after applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria to an initial dataset of 533 records.A bibliometric analysis was conducted using R Studio (Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation patterns, influential sources, country productivity, highly cited documents, keyword co-occurrence networks, and thematic structures within the research domain.The findings indicate a rapidly expanding body of research linking artificial intelligence and digital technologies with logistics service quality, customer satisfaction, e-commerce logistics, last-mile delivery, route optimization, and digital supply chain management.The field has experienced particularly strong growth after 2020, reaching its highest publication output in 2025.Customer satisfaction emerges as the most central keyword, suggesting that the literature remains strongly grounded in a service-quality and customer-experience perspective, even as advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, big data analytics, the Internet of Things, blockchain, automation, and optimization techniques become increasingly integrated into logistics service systems.Keyword co-occurrence analysis and thematic mapping are used as two complementary techniques.The keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies four major clusters representing distinct research streams, while thematic mapping reveals five thematic areas, reflecting different analytical logics underlying network-based clustering and centralitydensity-based classification.The study contributes to a clearer understanding of the intellectual structure of AI-driven logistics service quality research and provides future research directions related to customer experience, sustainable last-mile delivery, responsible AI adoption, and intelligent logistics service systems.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Competency-based medical education (CBME) emphasizes clinical reasoning as a core postgraduate competency, yet structured teaching strategies such as SNAPPS remain under-optimized in pediatric postgraduate training. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a supervised cognitive scaffold within SNAPPS, but empirical outcome-level evidence, particularly from pediatric postgraduate education in India, is limited. Objective To evaluate the effect of AI-assisted SNAPPS on clinical reasoning, structured case-presentation quality, and knowledge acquisition among pediatric postgraduate residents, and to assess learner and faculty perceptions of the intervention. Methods A prospective, single-arm, within-subject educational interventional study was conducted over six months among 30 pediatric postgraduate residents (10 each from JR1, JR2, and JR3) in the Department of Pediatrics, NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences & Research Centre and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur. Following sensitization, all participants underwent baseline assessment, a traditional-SNAPPS teaching phase, and an AI-assisted SNAPPS phase using a standardized SNAPPS-mapped AI prompt protocol with mandatory faculty validation at every step. Outcomes were measured using the Script Concordance Test (SCT), a validated 30-point SNAPPS analytical rubric, a multiple-choice question (MCQ) knowledge test, and five-point Likert perception surveys for residents and faculty. Paired comparisons were analyzed using appropriate parametric and non-parametric tests; p < 0.05 was considered significant. Results Mean SCT scores improved significantly with AI-assisted SNAPPS (12.0 ± 2.0 to 19.6 ± 2.8, p < 0.001), a gain that exceeded the improvement achieved with traditional SNAPPS alone (11.8 ± 2.1 to 15.2 ± 2.5, p < 0.01). The total SNAPPS rubric score rose from 19.1 ± 3.2 to 27.6 ± 2.9 (p < 0.001), with significant gains across all six domains. MCQ knowledge scores improved similarly (12.7 ± 2.5 to 18.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.001). SCT and SNAPPS rubric scores were strongly and positively correlated (r = 0.72, p < 0.001). Both residents and faculty reported significantly higher satisfaction with AI-assisted SNAPPS across every measured domain (all p < 0.001). Conclusion AI-assisted SNAPPS, implemented as a faculty-supervised cognitive scaffold, is feasible, well accepted, and educationally effective for strengthening clinical reasoning, structured presentation and knowledge retention among pediatric postgraduate residents. The model merits validation in larger, multicentric, competency-based curricula.

documents.abstract: This article examines the current state and prospects of using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in Ukraine's judicial system. It analyses the international and national regulatory and ethical benchmarks for the use of AI in judicial proceedings, in particular the provisions of Opinion No. 26 (2023) of the Consultative Council of European Judges, the European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment, and the CEPEJ Guidelines on the use of generative artificial intelligence for courts. The article also outlines Ukrainian organisational approaches, notably the Regulation on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies by Employees of the Office of the Supreme Court. The main focus is a review of case law on parties' use of generative AI output, references to fictitious court decisions and legal positions, and AI use in drafting judicial acts. The article argues that AI output has no independent evidentiary value and cannot replace the judge’s assessment of evidence, legal analysis or the reasoning of a court decision. It identifies the key risks of using AI: legal ‘hallucinations’, algorithmic bias, opacity, breaches of confidentiality, loss of professional autonomy, and unequal access to technology. Effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into Ukraine’s judicial system requires not only the formal enshrinement of relevant rules, but also the development of a coherent institutional culture of responsible use. The introduction of AI must be accompanied by uniform methodological guidelines for courts and participants in the judicial process, improved systems for verifying the authenticity of electronic sources, and mechanisms for verifying results obtained using generative models. Ensuring the digital literacy of judges, court staff, lawyers and other participants in the administration of justice is of particular importance, as it is precisely their level of awareness that determines the limits of the safe and ethical use of such technologies. At the same time, it is emphasised that the digitalisation of the justice system must not lead to the devaluation of the human element, a decline in trust in the judiciary, or the erosion of guarantees of a fair trial. The article concludes that the acceptable model for Ukraine is the assistive use of AI, under which technology supports administrative, analytical and information processes but does not take over the functions of the judge. It proposes ways of improving the legal framework: statutory definition of permitted and prohibited uses of AI, the introduction of standards for disclosing its use, and the provision of algorithmic audits, professional training for users and safeguards ensuring effective human oversight.

documents.abstract: This article examines the opportunities and risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence in the investigation of war crimes. The relevance of this topic stems from the significant increase in the volume of digital information that may hold evidentiary value—including photographs, video footage, satellite imagery, open-source data, social media content, electronic documents, and geolocation data. Processing such vast datasets using traditional methods requires substantial time and personnel resources, thereby necessitating the use of modern technological tools. This paper examines the primary applications of artificial intelligence in the collection, systematization, classification, and analysis of information related to war crimes. Particular attention is paid to the use of machine learning algorithms, computer vision, and natural language processing technologies for analyzing photographic, video, and textual materials; recognizing objects and individuals; establishing spatiotemporal links between events; and processing large datasets. The prospects for utilizing artificial intelligence in working with open-source intelligence (OSINT), digital evidence, and satellite imagery are also outlined. At the same time, the key risks associated with the use of such technologies have been analyzed. These include the potential for erroneous or biased results, the dependence of algorithms on the quality of input data, a lack of transparency in algorithmic decision-making processes, and violations of privacy and personal data protection. A distinct threat is posed by the proliferation of deepfake technologies capable of creating or altering digital content, which complicates the verification of its authenticity and reliability. It is argued that the outputs of artificial intelligence cannot be automatically accepted as reliable evidence and must undergo proper verification and procedural assessment. Artificial intelligence should be utilized as an auxiliary tool that enhances the speed and efficiency of investigators, prosecutors, and experts, without replacing their professional judgment. The study concludes that there is a need to improve legal regulation, develop unified standards for verifying digital evidence, and ensure appropriate human oversight regarding the use of artificial intelligence technologies in the investigation of war crimes.

Abstract Nigeria has the world’s largest electricity-access deficit, and unreliable grid supply drives demand for solar systems and for dependable after-sales technical support. This report examines how artificial intelligence can strengthen the technical support function of GVE Projects Ltd, a Nigerian solar energy company whose public contact model relies on telephone, e-mail and short online forms. It analyses the current support process and compares it with three reference cases: M-KOPA, Huawei FusionSolar smart diagnostics and GVE’s own pay-as-you-go mini-grids. Technical support is treated as a decision system, in which each contact ends in self-resolution, remote fix, field dispatch or specialist escalation. AI is introduced only where it improves one of these decisions and a human can override it. The report proposes a phased, human-supervised system with five architectural layers: WhatsApp-first customer intake, retrieval-augmented knowledge answers, rule-and-model fault triage with a confidence-gated decision rule, and optional telemetry-based predictive maintenance. The design includes an ArchiMate enterprise-architecture model, key performance indicators, a work breakdown structure, a twelve-month plan, a feasibility study, an ISO 31000:2018 risk evaluation and a five-year economic assessment. Because GVE’s internal data were unavailable, the as-is process and the economic model rest on public sources and stated assumptions, and a sensitivity analysis tests them. The report concludes that a narrow, compliance-first deployment under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is feasible, and that its success depends more on data quality and staff adoption than on the choice of AI model.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated into medical education globally, yet evidence from sub-Saharan Africa remains sparse. Postgraduate medical training institutions in this region face distinctive cultural, resource and infrastructure constraints that may shape how educators and trainees engage with AI. This study examined knowledge and self-reported use of AI among postgraduate medical residents and faculty in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted across three postgraduate medical training universities in Dar es Salaam the Aga Khan University (AKU), Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), and Hubert Kairuki Memorial University (HKMU). A census sampling approach was used, targeting all available residents and faculty. Data was collected via an online structured questionnaire assessing AI knowledge, exposure, and self-rated competence. Knowledge scores were derived from a ten-item questionnaire and compared across groups using Welch's t-test and multivariable linear regression to determine association with knowledge scores. Results A total of 155 participants participated in the study (116 residents, 39 faculty). Mean age group was 31–40 years. Formal AI training was rare (7.1%), yet 80.0% reported using AI in teaching or learning activities. Residents used AI substantially more than faculty (65.8% vs. 14.2%). Overall objective knowledge was moderate (mean score 59.0%, SD 18.2%), with no significant difference between residents and faculty (p = 0.623). Specialty was also associated with knowledge scores, with medical and radiology specialties outperforming non-clinical specialties Self-rated knowledge at Level 5 was the only independent predictor of higher objective scores in multivariable analysis (β = 0.151; 95% CI 0.022–0.302; p = 0.049). Conclusions AI use is widespread among postgraduate trainees in Dar es Salaam despite minimal formal training. Knowledge gaps are evident, particularly around foundational AI concepts. Self-perceived competence, rather than professional role or formal training, predicted objective knowledge. These findings underscore the need for structured, contextually adapted AI literacy curricula within postgraduate medical education in Tanzania and similar settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an important tool in social media marketing, enabling businesses to deliver personalized content and enhance consumer engagement. At the same time, growing environmental awareness has increased interest in green products. This study develops a conceptual framework to explain the relationship between AI-driven social media marketing, consumer trust, and green purchase intention in Uzbekistan. Based on recent literature, the proposed framework suggests that AI-driven social media marketing strengthens consumer trust and positively influences consumers' intention to purchase green products. The study contributes to the green marketing literature by integrating these constructs into a unified conceptual model and provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical research in Uzbekistan. In Outcome-Based Education (OBE) environments, student academic progressionrepresents a complex, non-linear dynamic system governed by multi-faceted indicatorsincluding performance trajectories, engagement metrics, and learningsupport mechanisms. Traditional evaluation methods often fail to capture time-dependentperformance risks and degradation patterns across successive assessmentstages. In this paper, we establish a novel reliability-based degradationmodeling framework that adapts engineering reliability principles and hazard-ratesurvival analysis to educational decision-support systems. Utilizing a standardized,publicly available academic progress dataset, our framework modelsperformance stability via cumulative reliability functions and identifies critical vulnerabilitythresholds using hazard-rate formulations. Students are classified intodistinct progression cohorts (high, moderate, and low achievers) based on normalizedperformance distributions. Empirical findings demonstrate a strong correlationbetween early academic stability and long-term progression reliability,showing that multi-year failing trajectories exhibit exponentially higher degradationrates. The proposed framework provides an interpretable, data-driven analyticaltool to monitor student risk, support early Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driveninterventions, and optimize institutional decision-making in modern outcome-based learning architectures.

As arts in transit has become an increasingly prominent practice in urban public transportation spaces worldwide, it is important to understand how AI-generated images are reshaping visual orders across different urban contexts. Taking Beijing Metro Line 2 as the primary case, supplemented by contextual observations on Lines 1, 4, and 10, this study draws on participant observation and semi-structured interviews. The findings reveal three interconnected changes. First, traditional transit art continues to provide durable cultural references, yet it faces growing competition from rapidly renewed visual content for limited passenger attention, producing a form of attentional displacement. Second, generative AI accelerates an already commercialized visual regime by lowering production costs, shortening revision cycles, increasing scalability, and redistributing authorship across algorithms, designers, and managers. Third, AI-generated imagery has expanded from advertising into public-service communication and cultural content, where it is incorporated into existing processes of institutional review and display. These changes reveal two dimensions of visual governance: institutional control over the production and display of visual content, and the organization of attention and spatial meaning through visual means. The Beijing Metro case therefore reconsiders the public value of arts in transit by showing how AI-driven visual production is reconfiguring the institutional, cultural, and perceptual conditions through which publicness is produced in urban transit space.

Purpose: The purpose of this paper is to examine the use of digital platforms to automate financial and management accounting functions, with particular focus on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technology. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a qualitative secondary data research methodology using existing scholarly materials, industry reports, and case studies to evaluate the effectiveness of these technologies in improving accounting operations. The sample of 27 publications (2014–2026) was obtained from online academic databases such as Google Scholar, ScienceDirect and JSTOR, and examined by thematic analysis. Research Limitation: The study identifies high implementation costs, technical complexity, and data privacy and cybersecurity issues as the main challenges, indicating the need for further research on scalable and cost-effective solutions. Findings: The findings indicate that AI-driven automation enhances precision, reduces human error, and supports more accurate decision-making through instant data analysis. Blockchain technology increases the transparency, security, and reliability of financial transactions through its decentralised and immutable structure. Practical Implication: The adoption of AI and blockchain in accounting systems offers considerable advantages for organisations, particularly in improving operational efficiency and supporting strategic management. Social Implication: The wider adoption of digital technologies contributes to more transparent, secure, and reliable accounting practices in the modern business environment. Originality/Value: The article examines AI and blockchain in management accounting tasks, such as forecasting and decision support, which have received less attention than auditing and financial reporting, and highlights future research directions for the development of scalable solutions that can be adopted at lower cost.

Abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, especially Generative AI, is really changing how we work and what employment looks like. While these AI technologies can boost productivity and enhance decision-making, they might also lessen the need for human workers in some roles, leading to layoffs and job losses. This shift has sparked worries about job security, potential layoffs, the need for reskilling, and whether current labor laws are adequate. This research examines whether the safeguards provide under Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act from 1947 are enough to protect employees whose jobs are impacted by automation and tech advancements. It zooms in on key legal protections related to layoffs, notice periods, compensation, required government approvals, and other employee safeguards. Additionally, it looks at the challenges posed by Generative AI, especially how tech changes can shift job roles, cut down the demand for certain skills, or even render some positions obsolete. The study takes a doctrinal and qualitative approach, pulling from a variety of sources like legislation, court rulings, academic research, government documents, and insights into AI, automation, and employment. It also examines the Industrial Relations Code of 2020 to grasp how India's labor law framework is evolving in light of technology. The findings indicate that while current labor laws do offer crucial protections during layoffs, they might not fully tackle the issues brought on by AI-related job changes. There's a strong suggestion that more focus is needed on reskilling, redeploying, transparency, and providing support during transitions before any layoffs occur. Therefore, the study advocates for a more employee-centered approach, encouraging employers to prioritize reskilling and redeployment ahead of layoffs, while also balancing tech advancements, business demands, and employee rights. 1. Introduction With the rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) and the AI-related industry, AI systems have come to core industrial and economic infrastructures. However, an appropriate redistribution structure for "knowledge creation" (such as academic papers and intellectual property)—which forms the foundation of AI learning and inference—and an autonomous mechanism connecting AI economic revenues to external social security and cultural redistributions have not yet been established. In this study, we propose the "Casino Protocol," a smart contract protocol that automatically collects a flat 1% from the revenue of AI-related companies and uses it as the source for "cultural redistribution (artist fees)," "autonomous driving insurance reserves" as social infrastructure, and "tuition fees (knowledge rewards)" for academic achievements (DOIs) and the origin node.

documents.abstract: Background: Among the health related problems, commercial sex is one of the leading occupational health problems in Bangladesh. To understand the health risks among female sex workers is very important. This risks may be due to work related problems and others. This study was done to understand the socio demographic profile, background of commercial sex and health related problems among the female sex workers. Materials and methods: The study was a cross-sectional study conducted during the period from 6th to 31st March 2026. A purposive sampling technique was applied to select 69 female sex workers and data were collected by face to face interview using a structured questionnaire. Obtained results were compiled and analyzed using SPSS version 23. Chi square test was done to see the association between socio demographic problem and background of commercial sex. Results: Among the 69 sex workers, 58(84.05%) respondents were aged between 25 to 40 years. Muslims were predominant in this study which constituted about 46(66.7%). Majority 60(87%) of the respondents were married. 38(55.1%) had primary level of education, 19(27.5%) were illiterate, 52(75.4%) came from nuclear family and 37(53.7%) belonged to lower middle class. 47(68.1%) had income ranging from TK. 20,000 to 50,000. Among the 69 study subjects, 55(79.7%) had joined in sex work at the age of 18-25 years and 14(20.3%) had started at the age of 25-40 years. 35(50.7%) were in this work for 1-5 years and 34(49.3%) were working for more than 5 years. All 69 were involved in other profession earlier. Regarding number of clients, it was seen that 21(30.4%) had 2 clients per day, 45(65.2%) had 3-5 clients and 3(4.3%) had more than 5 clients per day. All 69 respondents were involved in other professions. 38(55.1%) said they quitted previous job due to bad working condition, 9(13%) for personal issues, 8(11.6%) for family problems and 14(20.3%) for less income. 32(46.4%) joined sex work at their own wish, 30(43.5%) due to more income and 7(10.1%) were cheated and trapped in this profession. All the respondents of the current study knew about sexually transmitted diseases. 5(7%) suffered from hepatitis and 17(25%) suffered from scabies. 52(75.4%) said that they had a guilty feeling for joining sex work and 53(77%) wanted to quit sex. Conclusion: This study concluded that female sex workers got involved in sex work for more income and low socioeconomic status. Socio demographic factors were sensible to develop health risks. Increasing awareness and educational support might help to reduce the work-related health risks among female sex workers. IAHS Medical Journal Vol 9(1), June 2026; 39-43

The article deals with the lexical and stylistic analysis of three essays generated by artificial intelligence and one essay by a human author on the same topic. The differences in the lexical and expressive means that convey emotionality, evaluation, and the degree of subjectivity have been revealed. The functional styles of each essay produced by artificial intelligence have been identified. The conclusion is made that artificial intelligence does not draw clear boundaries between styles and genres of texts, between essays, in particular, for example, between the publicistic and literary styles, or between the colloquial and literary styles. It is claimed that at the current stage of the artificial intelligence development and application in generating texts of different styles, the problem lies in the AI’s failure to distinguish between functional styles and text genres. AI cannot generate words based on cultural, literary, linguistic, and other associations related to word play in the way a human can.

Abstract Interactive digital resources are widely used in anatomy education, but their development typically requires programming expertise or commercial software, and pre-existing resources may not match an educator’s specific teaching requirements. Large language models (LLMs) are now capable of generating functional web code from conversational prompts, creating the possibility of educators producing their own interactive simulations without programming experience. Using LLMs to generate simulations for anatomical education, rather than as tutoring or assessment aids, remains under-investigated. This brief report is a proof-of-concept workflow in which three LLM platforms (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, and Anthropic Claude) were provided with reviewed anatomy content and prompted to generate interactive, browser-based simulations. Ten single-file Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) simulations were produced covering cranial nerve lesion testing, the pupillary light and corneal reflexes, extraocular muscle testing, visual field defects, spinal cord syndromes, the circle of willis, and the urinary sphincter function system. The simulations incorporate AI (Artificial Intelligence)-generated anatomical images, adjustable lesion parameters, and scenario-based clinical reasoning. Iterative refinement was necessary to achieve accurate results, as the AI repeatedly made errors, including confusion between left and right orientations, inaccurate positioning of facial features, and the occasional generation of images instead of modifying the code as instructed. These challenges required multiple rounds of correction and careful human oversight to ensure the final output met the intended requirements. Preliminary simulation assessment and comments from Medicine Year 2 colleagues, Oxford AI Build club, learning technologist, Teaching demonstrators were encouraging regarding clarity and engagement, although no formal student evaluation of learning outcomes has yet been conducted. We conclude that LLMs can translate structured anatomical knowledge into functional interactive anatomy simulations and describe a replicable workflow, while emphasising that expert review remains indispensable.
