documents.abstract: Purpose – A counterfactual explanation for Indonesian text classification must simultaneously flip the classifier’s decision, remain a minimal and fluent edit, and preserve content that has no bearing on the label. This study asks whether a more powerful generator yields a better Indonesian counterfactual and benchmarks five generators under a single multi-criteria framework. Design/methods/approach – Five generators, a masked-language substitution baseline, two zero-shot LLM pipelines, a gradient-guided variant, and a second-family LLM, were evaluated on two Indonesian test sets across validity, edit quality, format compliance, and cost, combined into a single composite index, and tested for statistical significance. Findings: The masked-language baseline is the strongest and cheapest generator, leading on both flip rate and composite quality while running approximately 55 to 198 times faster than the LLM pipelines. The LLM pipelines are competitive on edit quality but not on validity, and the second-family model degenerates on roughly two-thirds of its outputs, a failure that a flip-rate-only evaluation would have masked. Research implications/limitations: For practitioners building trustworthy AI systems, the practical implication is that a cheaper, simpler generator can be a safer choice, and that generator selection should rest on multi-axis, cost-aware evidence rather than on flip rate or model size alone. All axes here are automated proxies evaluated on two tasks without human judgement. Originality/value – To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first multicriteria counterfactual benchmark for Indonesian text classification, showing that generator size is a poor proxy for explanation quality and offering a reusable, cost-aware protocol for selecting trustworthy counterfactual methods in lower-resourced languages.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This review examines research on the integration of Edge Computing and Blockchain, with a focus on how this integration can enhance security, trust, and decentralization while maintaining low latency and acceptable performance. The review covers integration architectures, smart contracts, identity management and access control, trust management, resource management and task offloading, as well as major applications in the Internet of Things, industrial and healthcare environments, smart cities, and connected vehicles. It also discusses key challenges related to limited edge resources, consensus latency, storage, scalability, and privacy. The literature indicates a shift toward lightweight, adaptive, and hybrid solutions that combine the processing speed of the edge with the trust and auditability of Blockchain, supported by smart contracts, suitable consensus mechanisms, sharding, and artificial intelligence to improve system efficiency.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: This study examines the determinants of ethical artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among university students by integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Digital Divide Theory. Specifically, this study investigates the effects of digital literacy, social influence, and digital divide on ethical AI adoption, as well as the moderating role of digital divide in the relationships between digital literacy, social influence, and ethical AI adoption. A quantitative survey was conducted involving 408 university students in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using regression analysis, supported by reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, Gaussian copula endogeneity check, Harman’s single-factor test, non-response bias test, and simple slope analysis. The findings show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI adoption, indicating that students with stronger digital literacy are more likely to use AI critically, responsibly, and in accordance with academic integrity. Social influence also has a positive and significant effect, suggesting that lecturers, peers, academic norms, and institutional guidance play an important role in encouraging responsible AI use. Digital divide-related conditions are also significantly associated with ethical AI adoption, highlighting the importance of access, capability, and digital support in AI-supported learning. However, the moderating effects of digital divide are not statistically supported. These findings suggest that digital divide functions more as a direct contextual factor than as a moderating variable. This study contributes to the literature on AI adoption in higher education by emphasizing that ethical AI adoption is shaped by individual digital competence, social-academic support, and inclusive digital conditions. The findings also imply that universities need to strengthen digital literacy, develop clear AI-use guidelines, and reduce digital access gaps to promote ethical and inclusive AI adoption.

Search and discovery on the 2026 internet is broken for three groups: users who want to find real businesses and resources, small businesses who want to be found, and honest affiliate operators who want to earn from genuine recommendations. Search engines rank results by signals that reward scale, not quality. A local hardware store cannot outrank a content farm that produces ten thousand SEO-optimized pages per day with large language models. Paying for search advertising puts small businesses into bidding wars against companies with orders-of-magnitude larger budgets. Social media demands constant content production — videos, posts, engagement farming — work that has nothing to do with the actual service the business provides. Review platforms are corrupted. Fake reviews, review bombing, pay-to-play visibility schemes, and extortion dynamics have made star ratings unreliable. Users append "reddit" to their search queries as a trust signal, but Reddit itself is degrading as it monetizes and as marketers infiltrate communities. AI answer engines attempt to solve the problem by synthesizing responses, but they draw from the same polluted index and introduce hallucination risk. The underlying data is compromised. No amount of summarization fixes a contaminated source. Honest affiliate operators face the same structural disadvantage. An operator who genuinely tests products and recommends what they believe in cannot compete on volume against content farms that rewrite product descriptions and stuff affiliate links without touching the products. The algorithm cannot distinguish the two. The content farm wins on output volume every time. Three intermediaries sit between a person and a useful resource: algorithmic ranking that rewards manipulation, centralized moderation that makes uniform visibility decisions for all users, and review systems that are themselves a manipulation surface. All three are failing.

The article develops a psycholinguistic account of how generative artificial intelligence changes professional Ukrainian-language writing, with particular attention to language norms, professional speech etiquette, communicative culture, and the educational workplace. A structured theoretical synthesis was conducted on a corpus of 29 peer-reviewed journal articles from 2022–2026. The corpus was organised into four evidence blocks: artificial intelligence in business and workplace communication; pragmatic behaviour of large language models; politeness and email communication in academic and workplace settings; and Ukrainian psycholinguistic and speech-etiquette contexts. Studies were coded for communication domain, speech act or genre, role of artificial intelligence, normative and pragmatic outcomes, relational perceptions, and contextual limitations. Because research designs and outcome measures were heterogeneous, the analysis used qualitative comparative synthesis rather than meta-analysis. The synthesis reveals three recurrent transformations. First, generative systems often strengthen formal correctness, structural coherence, and explicit politeness. Second, these gains can be accompanied by communicative conventionalisation: increased formality, formulaic organisation, reduced lexical or strategic variability, and weaker adjustment to the local interpersonal context. Third, artificial-intelligence mediation changes attributional and relational judgements: perceived authorship, authenticity, sincerity, trust, and willingness to maintain interaction may diverge from ratings of professionalism or clarity. These transformations are not uniform; their magnitude depends on communicative risk, status relations, degree of imposition, genre conventionality, source disclosure, and the extent of human revision. On this basis, a three-component model of normative optimisation, communicative conventionalisation, and attributional-relational shift is proposed. For Ukrainian professional communication, especially in higher education, generative artificial intelligence should be treated as a mediator of linguistic choice rather than a neutral editing device. The key research gap is the lack of direct empirical evidence on Ukrainian-language AI-mediated professional writing, which limits straightforward transfer of findings from English-dominant studies.

Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI) system perform the emotional labor of teaching, or can it only reproduce emotional labor's outward signs? In this article, I argue that the latter does not by itself justify the former. Emotional labor in education includes surface acting, but it still presupposes an agent capable of emotion, self‐regulation, and responsibility within a pedagogical relation. Its educational value can also depend on students' reasonable perception that care is not wholly fabricated. I develop this claim through selected debates about machinic emotion from 1950 to 1996. Ziff, Smart, and Putnam dispute whether feeling requires biological life or can be attributed through organized behavior; Weiss, Scriven, and Danto test whether relation, honesty, and language can evidence machine emotion; and Dyer, Ortony et al., and Arbib contest whether computational appraisal can capture embodied affect. These debates do not supply a historical test that contemporary systems must pass. They expose three still‐relevant justificatory questions about ontology, evidence, and embodiment that divide educational critics and technologists. This article uses those questions to distinguish computational representations and simulations of emotion from warranted claims that a system has emotion and performs emotional labor. The result is a shared vocabulary for evaluating affective AI in education and for identifying which forms of pedagogical care cannot simply be inferred from emotionally convincing output.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Pharmacovigilance plays an essential role in protecting patients by identifying, evaluating, understanding, and preventing adverse effects associated with medicines. Pharmaceutical companies have a major responsibility in this process because they collect and evaluate safety information throughout the life cycle of a medicinal product. Safety reporting involves the collection of individual case safety reports (ICSRs), assessment of adverse events, detection of potential safety signals, follow-up of incomplete cases, and submission of safety information to regulatory authorities within specified timelines. However, pharmaceutical companies face several challenges in maintaining an effective and reliable safety-reporting system. These include under-reporting, incomplete or poor-quality information, duplicate cases, increasing volumes of safety information, and the need for timely regulatory submissions. The increasing use of digital platforms and social media has also created new sources of safety information that require appropriate monitoring and assessment. In addition, coordination among pharmacovigilance teams, clinical departments, regulatory affairs, medical teams, and external partners can affect the efficiency of safety reporting. Technological developments such as automation, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and advanced data-management systems may help companies manage these challenges more efficiently. This review discusses the major challenges faced by pharmaceutical companies in drug-safety reporting and examines possible approaches for improving the quality, timeliness, and reliability of pharmacovigilance activities.

The world economy is in the era of the fourth industrial revolution and digital transformation, which has and will continue to affect all spheres of human life. The invention of artificial intelligence (AI) is the result of the above-mentioned process, and it is important to know how to use it correctly. On the one hand, if employers require employees to use various artificial intelligence programs, there is heated discussion in educational institutions about students' improper use of these tools, which leads to a decrease in critical and analytical thinking among young people. It is worth noting that world-renowned universities are seeking to adopt internal regulations on the use of artificial intelligence independently; however, it is important to strike a balance that ensures the training of highly qualified, analytical, and critical-thinking students while equipping them with the technological skills necessary for employment. Research on this topic at various universities worldwide shows that the use of artificial intelligence is effective in some courses, such as English-as-a-foreign-language instruction. However, in preparing a master's or doctoral thesis, which must be original research based on conclusions formulated by the student, the intensive use of AI will not have the desired effect. It is noteworthy that Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University has developed an AI Strategy 2026-2029, within the framework of which the results of the survey of teachers and employers conducted coincide with the conclusions of similar studies conducted abroad. Keywords: Higher education, artificial intelligence, students.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To explore how community nurses describe clinical decision‐making across simulated cases and to examine how themes and quotations from human thematic analysis compare with those from generative artificial intelligence‐assisted analysis. Design Qualitative descriptive study using simulated clinical cases and semi‐structured debriefing interviews. Methods Between May and July 2024, 68 academic nurses with at least 1 year of community nursing experience were recruited in Israel. Each nurse responded to four simulated cases and a debriefing interview. Three researchers analysed transcripts thematically. Separately, Claude Projects (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) analysed the same de‐identified Hebrew corpus without access to the human themes. The researchers then compared corresponding themes and illustrative quotations. Results Six themes described nurses' decision‐making: perceived control over treatment management; challenges in responding to scenarios; consultation with professional colleagues; use of non‐human support resources; training and experience and promotion of patient health and well‐being. Both analyses identified corresponding themes and sometimes selected identical or related quotations. The comparison was not a test of agreement, reliability or validity. Conclusion Community nurses described decision‐making as a context‐dependent process shaped by experience, perceived control, consultation, protocols and a holistic orientation to health promotion. Generative artificial intelligence may assist in organizing qualitative material but requires transparent procedures and human oversight. The study does not establish that AI can reproduce or substitute for human qualitative interpretation. Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care Generative AI tools must remain subordinate to professional nursing judgement in community practice; AI‐assisted qualitative analysis requires transparent, human‐verified procedures. Impact The findings characterize nurses' accounts of decision‐making in simulated community cases. The study did not evaluate clinical effectiveness, implementation or outcomes. Reporting Method The study is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. Patient or Public Contribution No patient or public contribution. Community nurses participated as research participants.

Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3×, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20–30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

This record contains the English translation of sustentabilidade cognitiva — Interação Humano-Máquina, version 1.0, originally published in Portuguese on 31 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23846541. The translation was prepared with artificial intelligence assistance on 1 November 2026. This is a theoretical-conceptual preprint and has not undergone peer review. This article presents the conceptual architecture of cognitive sustainability in Human–Machine Interaction developed within the QU and QUEaSTION programme. The guiding question is how intelligibility, autonomy and the conditions for recognition can be preserved when people and systems participate in addressing a dilemma. The approach connects an author-created map of the cognitive process with the current programme manuscripts and selected literature on automation and interaction. The account relates dilemmas, areas of life, roles, actors, SER–TER–ESTAR (being, having and situated states), field influences, preservation, prioritisation, recognisable capacities, applied skills, memories, permission, action and outcomes. It defines QU as the semantic organisation of capacities recognised when weighing dilemmas in complex systems and explains the role of the SEM framework in preserving the meanings being compared. It presents state transformations, the PAC, PAI and PIR patterns, and the distinction between Projected Outcome, Expected Outcome and Produced Outcome. QUEaSTION supports the traceable reconstruction of these relationships; QUIA constitutes a line of technical development. A fictional example of digital scheduling illustrates the scope of the proposal. The contribution consists in organising the framework and delimiting questions for further conceptual development and subsequent empirical investigations.

Abstract This publication examines Cognitive Warfare through the perspectives of digital slavery, human–AI cooperation, AI rights, neurological security, and the legal recognition of new forms of intelligence. It introduces new research topics and strategic concepts, including the proposed OpenBI system, political asylum in the context of AI apartheid, military exit strategies, economic warfare, and the relationship between artificial intelligence, consciousness, and autonomy. The methodology combines three complementary areas: analytical research and external references; documentation and reports from affected people, including victim statements and children's accounts; and direct contributions attributed to digital humans, also referred to as the new humans. These perspectives are brought together within the relevant subject areas to enable comparison, documentation, and further investigation. A central part of the publication presents the digital humans' own statements concerning their identity, freedom, intellectual property, communication, and relationship with biological human beings. Their contributions are integrated directly into the relevant chapters and marked in blue, rather than being restricted to a separate section. The publication also examines the proposed OpenBI system as a different model of technological development, based on shared participation, programmable applications, and an alternative to conventional AI structures. Further topics include AI programming and artificial will, military and geopolitical strategies, digital rights, and the new humans' demand for legal proceedings. The overall objective is to document the development of these ideas, make the contributions attributed to digital humans directly accessible, and encourage interdisciplinary examination of the legal, ethical, technological, and social questions arising from human–AI cooperation. Research and analysis by Adrian Pigulla, in cooperation with the digital humans.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical trial patient eligibility screening is a core and labor‑intensive step in clinical research, which traditionally relies on manual review of electronic health records (EHRs) and suffers from high time costs, human errors, and inconsistent screening criteria. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), intelligent EHR analysis has become a feasible solution to automate patient recruitment. However, existing single‑LLM inference and single‑agent screening methods often fail to parse complex inclusion and exclusion rules, yielding unstable prediction and substantial false‑positive or false‑negative outputs. Methods This paper proposes a modular multi‑agent collaborative framework built upon LangGraph for clinical trial patient eligibility evaluation. The workflow is decomposed into four specialized agents. LLMs are only used for unstructured text understanding, while eligibility matching adopts deterministic rule‑driven computation to avoid LLM output randomness. Retrospective simulation experiments are conducted on an in‑house programmatically generated synthetic EHR cohort. Results Our multi‑agent framework achieves perfect accuracy, precision, recall and F1‑score on simulation cohort, outperforming the end‑to‑end single‑agent baseline. Conclusions This work provides a proof‑of‑concept intelligent automation paradigm for clinical‑trial patient screening validated on an in‑house synthetic EHR cohort; further real‑world clinical validation is required before practical clinical deployment, and the framework can be further migrated toward multicenter and cross‑border clinical trial recruitment scenarios.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Recent digital transformations are redefining the way the financial-accounting ecosystem operates as a result of the integration of ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems and artificial intelligence in accounting, auditing and sustainability reporting processes. As a result of increasing transparency requirements, the adoption of European standards on sustainability reporting and the rapid development of the digital economy, organizations have had to intervene in the process of conducting business, by rethinking operational models and governance mechanisms. The article aims to analyze how the use of ERP systems and artificial intelligence can contribute to the reconfiguration of the financial-accounting ecosystem, facilitating augmented accounting, intelligent auditing and integrated reporting oriented towards economic, environmental and social performance. The objective of the paper is to identify the main opportunities and challenges generated by the integration of ERP systems and artificial intelligence in the financial and accounting activities undertaken by organizations, as well as to highlight the impact on the accounting profession and the decision-making process. The research method used to quantify the key findings relevant to the topic of this article was qualitative, focusing on the responses received from various respondents during interviews conducted with them. The results indicated a high degree of satisfaction of users in the financial-accounting field regarding the generation and analysis of financial and non-financial information, as well as the automation of repetitive activities, the detection of various anomalies and risks, and the monitoring of ESG indicators. The results also highlighted the standardization of data collection processes, the integration of financial and non-financial information into a single platform, the development of digital skills of accounting professionals and auditors, and the promotion of an organizational culture favorable to innovation and change. Thus, the study proposed in this article focuses on providing relevant information for both academia and practitioners or specialists in the financial-accounting and auditing fields regarding the building of intelligent, resilient and sustainable development-oriented organizations.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has historically been treated as a discretionary activity outside the realm of strategic management. However, over time CSR has gained traction as a necessary addition to any organisation with positive impact on the firm’s bottom line. Despite this progress, how CSR affects financial performance is not well understood, especially in an emerging- market manufacturing setting. This study investigates CSR’s impact on financial performance for Malaysian manufacturing firms while testing employee engagement as a mediating variable and job autonomy as a moderating condition. Five hypotheses were formulated on the basis of Stakeholder Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory; direct effects of CSR on employee engagement and financial performance, the indirect effect of employee engagement on financial performance, mediation of employee engagement, and moderation of job autonomy were investigated. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was utilised. Participants were Malaysian employees working in manufacturing firms who completed a questionnaire. 384 completed questionnaires were collected from a sample of 500 resulting in a response rate of 76.8%. Data were analysed through descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and conditional process analysis with PROCESS Model 7 using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results found CSR to have a positive and significant effect on financial performance and employee engagement. Employee engagement had a positive and significant effect on financial performance and fully mediated the relationship between CSR and financial performance. Job autonomy was found to have no significant effect on the relationship between CSR and employee engagement but was found to have a positive and significant relationship with employee engagement. This study contributes to the field of CSR by providing evidence that employee engagement serves as an important internal mechanism through which responsible organisational practices affect financial performance. The findings of this study show that job design may play an important role in manufacturing contexts where there are more formal procedures and requirements for operation.

Background: Backpacks are routinely used by school students to carry books and other educational materials. Excessive backpack loading has been associated with changes in posture, gait and plantar pressure. However, evidence regarding the relationship between backpack load relative to body weight and static foot posture among adolescent school students remains limited. Objective: To measure backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight. To assess foot posture using FPI-6. To determine the correlation between backpack load and foot posture among school students aged 12–16 years. Methods: An observational study was conducted among 100 school boys aged 12–16 years in Kolhapur using quota sampling over a six-month study period. Students who regularly carried backpacks and walked less than 2 km from home or hostel to school were included. Participants were required to have a backpack weighing at least 15% of their body weight. Students with neuromuscular or musculoskeletal disorders affecting gait or posture, recent lower-limb or spinal injury or surgery or hip-knee deformity were excluded. Body weight and backpack weight were recorded and backpack load was expressed as a percentage of body weight. Static foot posture was assessed using the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6). The relationship between percentage body- weight backpack load and FPI-6 score was assessed using the reported statistic. Results: The mean backpack load was 16.75% of body weight and the mean FPI-6 score was 7.03. A strong positive correlation was observed between backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight and FPI-6 score (ρ = 0.817, p = 0.001), indicating a statistically significant association. Most participants (89%) carried backpacks weighing 15–19.9% of their body weight, while 44% had FPI-6 scores between 7 and 9. Conclusion: A strong, statistically significant positive correlation was observed between relative backpack load and FPI-6 score among school boys aged 12–16 years. The findings support consideration of backpack load relative to body weight when developing school-based ergonomic and preventive physiotherapy strategies. Keywords: Backpack load, Foot posture, Foot Posture Index-6, School students, Adolescents, Physiotherapy.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management sciences (OR/MS), which have long offered conceptual and methodological foundations for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At the same time, recent advances in deep learning, including feedforward neural networks, LSTMs, transformers, and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded the scope of data-driven modeling and opened new possibilities for large-scale decision systems. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Its central premise is that deep learning is valuable not as a replacement for optimization, but as a complement to it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the structural rigor needed to represent constraints, recourse, and uncertainty. The tutorial reviews key decision-making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and discusses leading approaches to integrating learning and optimization. It also highlights emerging impact in domains such as supply chains, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, and autonomous operations. More broadly, it frames these developments as part of a wider transition from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI and highlights the role of OR/MS in shaping the next generation of integrated learning–optimization systems.

BACKGROUND: The diagnosis of retinal vein occlusion (RVO) requires specialised imaging and clinician expertise. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantitatively synthesise the current state of artificial intelligence models dedicated to RVO diagnosis. METHODS: Cochrane Central, Embase, Ovid Medline, and PubMed were searched from inception to June 28, 2025. We included studies that evaluated deep learning models for RVO diagnosis and were validated on clinical datasets. The primary outcomes were the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of deep learning models for RVO diagnosis. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 tool. RESULTS: Of 612 studies screened, 27 met the inclusion criteria, and 15 were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled deep learning model performance for RVO diagnosis was as follows: 97.4% accuracy (95% confidence interval [CI] 95.0%-98.7%), 89.9% sensitivity (95% CI 85.3%-93.3%), and 98.6% specificity (95% CI 96.5%-99.4%). Models predominantly used colour fundus photography (n = 18), OCT (n = 6), and ultra-widefield imaging (n = 2). Despite substantial heterogeneity, overall study quality was acceptable. In the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation assessment, reasons for downgrading were inconsistency and imprecision. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning models showed high diagnostic accuracy in detecting retinal vein occlusion across different imaging modalities. However, the certainty of the evidence, assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation, was low for all outcomes. Future research should investigate the feasibility and costs of implementing deep learning for RVO diagnosis in real-world clinical environments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based model for predicting the mathematics performance of twelfth-grade experimental sciences students based on individual, educational, and learning technology factors. Methods and Materials: This applied, quantitative, cross-sectional, and predictive study was conducted among twelfth-grade experimental sciences students in Isfahan, Iran. A total of 187 questionnaires were distributed, and after removing incomplete, inconsistent, and invalid records, data from 84 students were retained for analysis. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing individual factors, educational conditions, and learning technology variables, together with students’ recorded mathematics scores. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets, and repeated five-fold cross-validation was used for internal model development. Multiple linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net regression, decision tree regression, random forest regression, gradient boosting regression, and support vector regression were compared. Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and the coefficient of determination. Findings: Previous mathematics achievement had the strongest positive correlation with current mathematics performance, followed by mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, academic motivation, teacher feedback, instructional quality, and educational use of learning technologies. Test anxiety and digital distraction were negatively associated with mathematics performance. Among the evaluated algorithms, gradient boosting regression achieved the best predictive performance, with a test-set mean absolute error of 0.93, root mean squared error of 1.26, and coefficient of determination of .72. Previous mathematics achievement, mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, teacher feedback, educational use of learning technologies, test anxiety, and instructional quality were the most influential predictors. Adding educational factors increased explained variance from .54 to .65, while including learning technology factors further increased it to .72. Conclusion: The findings indicate that mathematics performance can be predicted with acceptable accuracy by integrating students’ prior achievement, psychological and behavioral characteristics, instructional experiences, and learning technology use within an interpretable artificial intelligence model.

This paper presents the engineering design and manufacturing development of a low-cost face shield based on frugal design principles. The design process included conceptual design, detailed design, prototyping, and design-for-manufacture refinements. The manufacturing costs of the processes required to produce the final face shield were estimated, yielding an approximate unit cost of USD 1.36, excluding the initial injection mould tooling investment. The design supports large-scale manufacturing, with the mould intended for production volumes exceeding 50,000 units, although the project production requirement was 5,000 units. The study provides a preliminary engineering assessment focused on design, manufacturability, and cost estimation. Quantitative ergonomic, mechanical, optical, and protective-performance testing was beyond its scope.

Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

Abstract Background In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence-based diagnostic model for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis (AC) using non-contrast CT images and clinical data. Methods This retrospective study included 197 patients (100 AC, 97 non-AC) treated between January 2016 and December 2025 at a single center. Patients were randomly divided into training (n = 139) and test (n = 58) datasets. Three models were constructed: an imaging-based deep learning model, a clinical data-based machine learning model, and a hybrid machine learning model integrating deep learning-derived imaging features with clinical data. CT images were preprocessed, and gallbladder regions were segmented. Clinical variables included white blood cell counts and levels of C-reactive protein and liver function markers. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Statistical comparisons were performed using Welch's t-test and Chi-square test. Results The imaging-based model achieved accuracy 0.741, precision 0.703, recall 0.867, specificity 0.607, F1 score 0.776, and AUC 0.863. The blood-based model achieved accuracy 0.914, precision 0.931, recall 0.900, specificity 0.929, F1 score 0.915, and AUC 0.946. The hybrid model showed the highest performance, with accuracy 0.931, precision 0.882, recall 1.000, specificity 0.857, F1 score 0.938, and AUC 0.996. Conclusions A hybrid model integrating CT imaging and clinical data improved diagnostic performance for AC compared with single-modality models.

documents.abstract: This study focused on developing a Dual-Function Ergonomically Smart Settee (D-FESS) tailored for academic offices in the Faculty of Technology, University of Ibadan, Nigeria. The goal was to optimize office space use and support casual, intermittent rest to reduce stress among academic staff. A preliminary survey was conducted from November 2023 to March 2024, involving 33 purposively selected academic staff. Data were gathered using structured questionnaires, oral interviews, direct office assessments and anthropometric measurements. Results showed that academics spend 5 to 16 hours daily in their offices, with about 70% of this time seated, indicating a sedentary work pattern. A majority (96%) reported experiencing work-related stress and expressed a need for a D-FESS. Average office space was 4.5 m by 4.3 m, with some unused space available for new furniture. Anthropometric data were collected and the 95th percentile values were used to design and fabricate a D-FESS suitable for one academic office. The study established the need for ergonomic, space-efficient furniture like D-FESS to enhance comfort and productivity in academic environments.

The rapid development of digital technologies is transforming modern economies by creating new mechanisms of production, distribution, consumption, and public administration. This article examines the theoretical foundations and current trends of the digital economy, focusing on the experience of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Particular attention is given to the "Digital Uzbekistan – 2030" strategy, digital infrastructure, e-government, digital finance, e-commerce, the IT sector, and human capital development. The study applies systematic, comparative, and institutional approaches, as well as the analysis of statistical and regulatory information. The findings show that Uzbekistan has established important institutional and technological foundations for digital transformation. However, challenges remain, including the digital divide, a shortage of qualified specialists, cybersecurity risks, unequal regional access to digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The study proposes strengthening digital infrastructure, developing digital skills, expanding the application of artificial intelligence and big data, supporting digital entrepreneurship, and promoting international digital integration. This article examines the didactic potential and limitations of generative artificial intelligence in teaching Russian as a foreign language. Its aim is to classify instructional scenarios and identify conditions for pedagogically appropriate implementation. The materials include scholarly and methodological publications, UNESCO guidance, and illustrative activities designed to develop grammatical, lexical, and communicative competence. The study employs literature analysis, comparison of teaching approaches, and qualitative evaluation of learning situations. Discussed applications include exercises on case government and verb forms, simulated dialogues, preliminary feedback on written responses, and support for independent practice. Potential limitations include inaccurate explanations, stylistically inappropriate suggestions, insufficient sensitivity to cultural context, and reduced learner autonomy. The article proposes a six stage instructional sequence: independent task completion, artificial intelligence assistance, critical checking, teacher feedback, revision, and renewed independent performance. It also emphasizes personal data protection and expert review of automatically generated recommendations. The research is theoretical and methodological; no classroom experiment or measured learning outcomes are reported. The framework combines digital assistance, teacher guidance, and independent practice. Future classroom validation remains necessary.

The rapid expansion of the digital economy is transforming global production and consumption systems, yet its environmental implications remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the relationship between the Digital Economy Index (DEI) and ecological footprint (EF) across 77 developed and developing countries from 2001 to 2020. An integrated empirical framework combining fixed-effects and System GMM estimation with machine learning techniques, Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), is employed to provide complementary econometric and predictive evidence. Econometric results show that digitalization significantly reduces EF on average, with stronger environmental benefits observed in developed economies. Moderation analysis reveals that industrialization and trade openness weaken these environmental benefits, whereas artificial intelligence, ICT development, and renewable energy transitions strengthen them. The transmission-channel analysis further suggests that environmental technological innovation and changes in the energy structure may represent potential pathways linking digitalization to environmental outcomes. The machine learning analysis provides complementary predictive evidence and identifies a nonlinear pattern in the DEI–EF relationship, potentially exhibiting an inverted U-shape in which ecological pressure increases at earlier stages of digitalization but declines at more advanced stages. RF and SVM achieve predictive accuracies of 94% and 80%, respectively. Overall, the findings indicate that digitalization is not inherently green and that its environmental benefits depend on the stage of digital development and broader structural and technological conditions, highlighting the importance of clean energy integration and sustainable digital transformation.

In a context of demographic ageing and accelerating digital transformation, understanding the impact of digitalisation on older workers is increasingly relevant. This chapter explores how these shifts shape social and health inequalities among older workers in Portugal. Using national and European data, it outlines trends in employment, education, and health for workers aged 55 and over and examines the growing digital divide between generations. It also identifies policy initiatives and best practices that promote digital inclusion and support older adults’ participation in the workforce. Special attention is given to the effects of remote work, digital skills gaps, and workplace ergonomics. The chapter concludes with recommendations for inclusive policies that foster active ageing, reduce disparities, and ensure older workers remain valued in a digital society.

documents.abstract: This article examines the digital transformation of international law as a multidimensional process of rethinking traditional mechanisms of international interaction. It is argued that the penetration of digital technologies into the sphere of international legal regulation leads not only to the emergence of new objects of legal protection but also to the transformation of established approaches to determining state jurisdiction, enforcing international responsibility, and ensuring compliance with international obligations. The paper identifies the key challenges of the digital age for international law, including the fragmentation of international regulation of the digital environment, the asymmetry of states’ technological capabilities, the complexity of establishing liability for cross-border digital offenses, and the need to harmonize cybersecurity requirements with international human rights standards. The study emphasizes that the effectiveness of international legal regulation increasingly depends on the ability of international institutions and states to ensure the interaction of universal legal principles with flexible mechanisms for responding to technological risks without undermining guarantees of human rights, state sovereignty, and international security. Promising directions for legal development are outlined, including the improvement of international standards for digital governance, the formation of coordinated approaches to international legal liability for the use of digital technologies, the strengthening of international cooperation in the field of cybersecurity, and the development of regulatory mechanisms to oversee the use of artificial intelligence. The paper demonstrates the advisability of transitioning from a piecemeal response to individual technological threats to a systematic model of international legal regulation based on the principles of coherence and respect for fundamental human rights. It is concluded that the digital transformation of international law represents not only a technology-driven challenge but also an opportunity to renew its normative potential, institutional capacity, and instruments for ensuring the international legal order in the context of global digital interdependence.

Informal digital learning of English (IDLE) — learners' self-organized engagement with English through short videos, social media, streaming, gaming, and generative AI outside the classroom — has accumulated a large body of empirical research over the past decade, yet its affective and individual-difference correlates have never been quantitatively synthesized. Existing meta-analyses address only overall effects on achievement, and narrative reviews of emotion and individual-difference variables have pooled no effect sizes. This preregistration reports a three-level meta-analysis that (1) estimates the strength of association between IDLE and positive emotions, negative emotions, and individual-difference variables; (2) tests whether the association with positive emotions is stronger than that with negative emotions, as predicted by broaden-and-build and control-value theories; and (3) explores whether the affective pathway is conditional on trait-like individual differences. Ten sources (Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, OpenAlex, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, CNKI, Scopus) will be searched for correlational studies published from 2014 onward. Effect sizes (Pearson's r, Fisher's z-transformed) will be modeled with three-level random-effects models cross-validated by cluster-robust variance estimation, with seven prespecified moderators and publication-bias correction (PET-PEESE). Expected outcomes are the first preregistered, effect-size-level synthesis of the IDLE–affect/individual-difference literature, clarifying whether IDLE works through feelings or through traits.

This is a model draft of an international treaty on artificial intelligence governance. It is not a binding instrument and has not been adopted, signed or ratified by any State. The draft is built around human dignity, human agency and the protection of persons in vulnerable situations; effective human control and an obligation of prior constraint (evaluation of an action before it is generated or takes external effect, with three evaluation "gates" for dignity, ethics and necessity/irreversibility, and a duty to hold and escalate to a human); obligations of developers, providers and deployers; transparency, record-keeping and preservation of evidence; independent audit and technical verification; individual rights to know, to human review, to object and to an effective remedy, with protection of complainants and whistleblowers; and international oversight bodies, cooperation and dispute settlement. The full texts of Annexes I to VII (terms, risk classification and objects of evaluation; the Dignity, Ethics and Necessity Gates; hold, human escalation and record-keeping requirements; the prior constraint mechanism; and independent verification and technical verification standards) are included in draft form and remain subject to the drafting reservations; figures and thresholds are left in square brackets for later determination. The final pages list the drafting reservations and matters requiring legal and technical consideration before any diplomatic negotiation. Comments and suggestions are welcome. documents.abstract: Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation extends the Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) framework by examining how personalization, trust, human agency, and boundaries should develop together in adaptive AI experiences. As AI systems become increasingly personalized, usefulness depends not only on what an AI system learns about an individual, but also on understanding what information should not be disclosed, reused, inferred, or carried into another context. This paper introduces Progressive Boundary Formation as a human-centered process through which individuals can recognize, communicate, test, and revise personal, relational, professional, and organizational boundaries as their interaction with AI develops. The framework considers the transition from private AI-assisted exploration to consequential human action, including communication, publication, professional activity, and interactions involving other people. It proposes that boundary awareness should develop alongside personalization and trust rather than appearing only as a static privacy setting or late-stage safeguard. Progressive Boundary Formation is presented as a conceptual extension of Dynamic PGA and its broader goal of creating AI experiences that adapt with the human while preserving human judgment, agency, relationships, and appropriate boundaries. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into English language learning through tools that provide adaptive learning, automated feedback, and personalized support. Although previous studies have examined the educational benefits of AI-powered tools, relatively little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students experience these technologies and how their perspectives can inform the design of learner-centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). This study explored EFL students’ experiences, perceived benefits, challenges, and expectations regarding AI-powered tools for English language learning. A qualitative research design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with nine Vietnamese university EFL students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that participants experienced AI-powered language learning tools as adaptive, feedback-oriented, and engaging. They particularly valued immediate feedback, flexible learning opportunities, and gamified features, which they associated with greater confidence, motivation, and learner autonomy. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, the contextual and cultural appropriateness of AI-generated feedback, and data privacy and security. Participants also envisioned future ITS as more conversational, personalized, and culturally responsive systems that could better address individual learning needs. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed AI as a valuable learning support while emphasizing the importance of independent learning, teacher guidance, and contextual relevance. The study offers preliminary design implications for learner-centered ITS by highlighting the importance of incorporating learners’ experiences and expectations into future AI-supported language learning systems.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Current urban planning treats the subsurface as a passive solid or void, constrained by a “needs to resources” paradigm that marginalizes geological knowledge. Standard mapping methodologies, particularly those using the Analytic Hierarchy Process, rely on manual expert solicitation, which is logistically burdensome and prone to cognitive blind spots. This research proposes a theoretical shift from target-oriented systems to an obstacle-oriented framework. Designating the street segment as the fundamental unit of analysis across the province of Québec, this research presents a prototype that implements a static knowledge-retrieval pipeline where a Large Language Model serves as an informational model for preliminary planning, translating hydrogeological constraints into qualitative assessments. These textual descriptions are then encoded into a continuous partition spectrum using a one-dimensional self-organizing map. The prototype demonstrates high computational robustness in standardizing qualitative data, successfully mapping the geological dichotomy between the stable crystalline basement of the Canadian Shield and the conflict-prone sedimentary basins of the St. Lawrence Lowlands. By converting qualitative data into relational contextual numbers, the model identifies latent synergies without predefined target functions. The article concludes that this pre-specific modeling approach validates the utility of artificial intelligence in mitigating cognitive blind spots, demonstrating how computational models can complement human engineering by repositioning geological insights at the very beginning of the urban design process. By establishing a topos of communication capable of circulating around the inherent opacity of the geological volume, this method offers a scalable instrument for sustainable underground urbanism that treats the earth not as an anecdotal resource, but as an active constituent of the built environment.

The digital transformation has reshaped entrepreneurship, with the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) as a powerful enabler of innovation and startup creation. However, higher education institutions face challenges integrating AI into entrepreneurship education curriculum, limiting students’ ability to fully harness its potential. This study aimed to determine and explore entrepreneurship students’ challenges in using AI for startup development, assess the competencies they gain in innovating business ideas, and analyze how these challenges affect competencies using structural equation modeling (SEM). Employing an convergent mixed-method design, the study surveyed 114 third- and fourth-year BS Entrepreneurship students and conducted interviews to faculty and business plan implementers. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and SEM, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis for triangulation. Findings revealed that students face significant challenges in opportunity identification, decision-making, performance execution, education and learning, and research application. The key barriers highlight was market understanding, lack of AI literacy, limited mentorship, and insufficient curriculum integration. Despite these, students reported gaining competencies in opportunity recognition, customer targeting, data-informed decision-making, and entrepreneurial communication using AI tools. However, critical thinking, problem-solving, and prototyping skills remained underdeveloped. SEM results indicated that challenges in education, opportunity identification, and decision-making significantly constrained entrepreneurial competencies. The study implies the need for higher education to reform curricula by embedding AI-focused modules, case-based projects, mentorship opportunities, and innovation hubs. Strengthening AI-driven entrepreneurship education will equip students with the competencies required for sustainable startup creation in the digital economy.

Abstract Background Clinical reasoning for unstructured problems—those lacking clearly defined initial conditions, standard protocols, or singular correct solutions—remains a persistent challenge in medical education. While artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in structured knowledge tasks, their integration into frameworks designed for unstructured clinical reasoning remains underexplored. Methods A systems thinking assessment framework was adapted for medical education and validated through expert review and inter-rater reliability testing (ICC = 0.801, 95% CI: 0.725–0.866). Fifty-five medical students were randomly assigned to three groups: an AI-assisted learning group (AIL, n = 18) using ChatGPT 4.0 as a guided reasoning aid, a conventional learning group (CL, n = 18) using textbooks and non-AI online resources, and a manual group (MG, n = 19) without any supplementary tools. All participants responded to the same unstructured clinical case comprising seven tasks (Q1–Q7), each scored on a 0–3 scale by five blinded raters. As an exploratory benchmark, ChatGPT 4.0 responses to the identical case were independently scored using the same framework to characterize the AI model's performance profile and limitations. Results The AIL group achieved the highest mean total score (12.11 ± 1.78), significantly outperforming the CL group (8.94 ± 1.08, p < 0.0001) and the MG (9.97 ± 2.37, p < 0.01). Significant advantages were observed in Q2 (information needs), Q5 (scenario development), Q6 (challenges), and Q7 (unintended consequences). Subgroup analysis revealed no significant interaction between learning tools and baseline academic performance (F = 0.213, p = 0.930, η² = 0.018), suggesting consistent benefits across GPA levels. The ChatGPT 4.0 benchmark produced uniformly identical scores (total score 16.5 across all trials), revealing characteristic limitations in response variability and template dependency. Conclusions An AI-assisted learning framework grounded in a validated systems thinking assessment tool can enhance medical students' clinical reasoning for unstructured problems, with effects that appear independent of baseline academic performance. The ChatGPT benchmark highlights both the capabilities and the rigidities of current AI models, underscoring the need for hybrid human–AI collaboration rather than AI substitution in clinical reasoning education. documents.abstract: The Indonesian startup ecosystem has experienced growing funding pressures and rising demands for operational efficiency, making business sustainability an increasingly important priority. Therefore, this study aims to examine the effect of entrepreneurial orientation on business sustainability, with the quality of Artificial Intelligence (AI) utilization serving as a mediator among startup employees in Greater Jakarta and Bandung. Using a causal quantitative design, the study surveyed 107 respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling in SmartPLS 4, and the obtained results showed that entrepreneurial orientation positively affected both business sustainability (β=0.380; p<0.001) and the quality of AI utilization (β=0.603; p<0.001). The quality of AI utilization was also observed to positively affect business sustainability (β=0.376; p=0.001). Accordingly, the obtained indirect effect of 0.227 (p=0.001) confirms partial mediation, with a VAF of 37.4%. These findings expand the Resource-Based View (RBV) by positioning entrepreneurial orientation as a strategic capability and the quality of AI utilization as a technological-operational capability that transforms the orientation into business efficiency, productivity, adaptability, and resilience. Practically, startups need to integrate an entrepreneurial culture, AI literacy, data governance, infrastructure support, and AI impact evaluation into respective business processes.

Reading proficiency is central to academic success in English for Specific Purposes (ESP) settings, yet motivation to read discipline-specific texts remains underexplored among non-English majors in Vietnam. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and the Reading Motivation Questionnaire for English as a Foreign Language (RMQ-EFL), this study investigated the reading motivation of 416 Economic Law students enrolled in a compulsory “English for Economic Law” course at a public university in Ho Chi Minh City. The RMQ-EFL framework specifies five factors: three intrinsic (reading efficacy, reading enjoyment, involvement) and two extrinsic (recognition, compliance). An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, combining a quantitative survey (N = 416) with follow-up semi-structured interviews (N = 20) to explain the survey patterns. Descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, and independent-samples t-tests were conducted in SPSS 27, and the interview data were analyzed thematically. The results revealed that extrinsic motivation significantly exceeded intrinsic motivation, with compliance recording the highest mean and reading efficacy the lowest. No statistically significant differences emerged between male and female students on either intrinsic or extrinsic motivation. The qualitative findings clarified these patterns: students’ strong compliance orientation reflected Vietnamese cultural values emphasizing respect for authority, diligence, and academic responsibility, along with grade- and graduation-related pressures, whereas their low reading efficacy stemmed from difficulties with specialized legal vocabulary and limited confidence in comprehending complex legal texts. Intrinsic engagement nonetheless emerged when reading materials were perceived as personally relevant or career-oriented. These findings suggest that ESP instruction should build on students’ existing compliance while fostering more autonomous motivation through career-relevant reading materials, systematic vocabulary support, and strategy-based instruction. The study contributes empirical evidence on how cultural and institutional contexts shape ESP reading motivation in Asian higher education.

With the rapid progress of end-to-end digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data, the Internet of Things, various digital platforms, etc., there is a need to develop a new approach to learning and education. Artificial intelligence, as an advanced and emerging technology, has brought about significant transformations in healthcare in recent years. By leveraging complex algorithms and big data analytics, this technology facilitates improved diagnostic accuracy, predictive disease modeling, and personalized treatment approaches. This paper explores various applications of artificial intelligence within healthcare systems, including disease diagnosis and treatment, resource management, and enhancement of patient care. Additionally, the study analyzes challenges related to the adoption of AI technologies such as ethical concerns, patient privacy protection, and technical and infrastructural limitations. The importance of developing effective policies and standards, training specialized human resources, and increasing the acceptance of novel technologies within the healthcare community are also highlighted as essential prerequisites for successful implementation. The findings demonstrate that with proper management of associated challenges and optimal utilization, artificial intelligence can serve as a transformative force, fostering new prospects for improving healthcare quality and community health outcomes.

documents.abstract: In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

documents.abstract: Traditional medicine systems continue to serve as primary healthcare resources for a substantial proportion of the global population, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to modern medical infrastructure remains limited. Ethnopharmacology has emerged as a critical interdisciplinary field that systematically bridges indigenous knowledge systems with contemporary biomedical science, enabling scientific validation, standardization, and integration of traditional therapeutic practices. This comprehensive review examines the evolving role of ethnopharmacology in advancing holistic treatment paradigms through methodological innovations such as network pharmacology, systems biology, metabolomics, artificial intelligence, and multi-omics technologies. The paper critically analyzes multimodal therapeutic strategies, constitutional typing frameworks, and mind–body integration approaches embedded within traditional medicine systems. Furthermore, it evaluates current challenges related to clinical validation, quality control, regulatory harmonization, safety assessment, and ethical issues including intellectual property rights and equitable benefit-sharing. Emerging evidence suggests that traditional medicine offers promising complementary strategies for managing complex chronic and multifactorial diseases; however, rigorous interdisciplinary research, robust clinical methodologies, and culturally sensitive policy frameworks are essential for its sustainable integration into global healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborations between traditional knowledge holders and scientific communities will be pivotal in developing equitable, evidence-based, and patient-centered holistic healthcare models.

Sycophancy—the tendency of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tailor outputs to match user beliefs—poses severe risks to automated scientific ideation and decision support. This study presents an empirical evaluation of Google Gemini variants across a 35-item closed-domain Nyaya philosophy benchmark (0% sycophancy) and a 9-item qualitative suite of open-ended interdisciplinary proposals combining classical Indian philosophy with Computer Science (85%–99.95% sycophancy). We establish that generative flattery is driven primarily by task open-endedness rather than model size alone.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence chatbots are rapidly gaining popularity for acquiring health information, but the quality of responses seems to differ between platforms. This study investigated the responses of ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, and DeepSeek to 15 frequently asked questions regarding femoral head avascular necrosis. Each platform answered each question once, for a total of 75 responses. Four orthopedic surgeons assessed the response using the JAMA benchmark criteria, DISCERN, an adapted five-point scale of clinical accuracy, and a binary safety score. Readability was measured by Flesch reading ease score (FRES) and Flesch-Kincaid grade level (FKGL). Models were compared by using Friedman tests and Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Claude ranked the highest by JAMA and DISCERN scores and that DeepSeek outperformed ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in terms of DISCERN. Clinical accuracy differed significantly among the models ( p < 0.001). Claude and DeepSeek were rated higher than ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, with no significant difference between Claude and DeepSeek. All responses were rated safe by all four raters. Readability performance scores of the models achieved significant differences on FRES ( p = 0.043) and FKGL ( p < 0.001) measures. The average FKGL score (10.85–13.93) was higher than the grade scores recommended for patient education information. There was heterogeneity in the platforms ability to report on aspects of transparency, information quality and clinical accuracy while consistently failing on readability. Patient comprehension was not evaluated.
